t: #3463 Check If Digits Are Equal After Operations II — Binomial Coefficients mod 10
o: Each operation replaces the digit row by its adjacent sums, which is exactly a convolution with [1,1]. After n−2 rounds the digit at final position i is Σⱼ dⱼ·C(n−2, j−i) mod 10 (verify on "3902": coefficients C(2,·) give 3+2·9=21→1 and 9+2·2=13→3? no — position 1 collects C(2,0)·9 + C(2,2)·2 = 11→1, matching "11"). So we just need binomials C(m, k) mod 10 for m up to 1e5, computed via Lucas theorem mod 5 plus the Kummer/Lucas bit-trick mod 2, then CRT-combined.
k: After t rounds, entry i equals Σⱼ C(t, j−i)·dⱼ mod 10 — Pascal's rule is the same recurrence.
C(m,k) is odd iff k's bits are a subset of m's bits (k & ~m == 0).
Mod 5 comes from Lucas' theorem digit by digit in base 5; CRT merges residues mod 2 and 5 into mod 10.

a.i: Literally perform the reductions. Beautifully simple and correct, but O(n²) time — fine to explain, doomed at n = 1e5.
s: Repeatedly replace the list by adjacent sums mod 10 until length 2.
a.t: O(n²) — each round shrinks the row by one

a.i: Compute S₀ = Σ dⱼ·C(m, j) and S₁ = Σ dⱼ·C(m, j−1) mod 10 with m = n−2. Each needed binomial mod 10 is rebuilt from its residues mod 2 (bit-subset test) and mod 5 (Lucas over base-5 digits of m), giving O(log m) per coefficient.
s: Precompute the base-5 digits of m and a 5×5 table of small binomials mod 5.
c5(k): Lucas — multiply table entries while digits of k stay ≤ digits of m, else 0.
c10(k): CRT-merge c5(k) with the parity bit (k & ~m == 0).
Accumulate S₀ and S₁ mod 10 and compare.
a.t: O(n log n) — two Lucas evaluations per digit, each O(log m)

w: Lead with the convolution observation — it converts a simulation problem into number theory. The mod-2 shortcut (Lucas ⇒ bit-subset) and base-5 Lucas are the two tools to name explicitly. Pitfall: getting the index direction wrong (coefficient C(m, j−i), not i−j) — always validate on "3902". Follow-up: generalize to mod p for arbitrary p, or output the final two digits.
